mainTopic: Documents that 'should never have been written' (לא ניתן ליכתב), and fixing prices and borrowing produce by the market rate without רבית
overview: The amud opens at the end of an argument about a sale document. Someone argues that a document the seller admits to should collect from נכסים משועבדים, just like a loan שטר the borrower admits writing. רבא answers that a document only has that power if it records something that was allowed to be written (ניתן ליכתב). רבינא tests this twice: once from רבי יוחנן's rule on a backdated document (שטר מוקדם), and once from a ברייתא about a robber who sold a stolen field. מרימר and the גמרא answer that the backdated document is still good from its true date. They also answer that the robber will make peace with the owner and make his sale document good. A new משנה then teaches that you may not fix a price now for produce delivered later until the market price is out, with exceptions for goods that are almost ready and for manure. The גמרא limits רבי יוחנן's ban to unsteady small-town markets. A ברייתא and רב נחמן discuss separate prices for new and old grain and for gleaners' wheat. רב הונא first forbade borrowing produce based on the market rate, then allowed it after hearing רבי אלעזר. The amud ends by setting up a new ברייתא about buying a traveler's package at the price of the town he is heading to, and its ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Proof from a borrower who admits he wrote the loan document
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an argument: if the borrower admits he wrote the document, the lender can collect even from sold properties. The same should be true here.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person admits that he wrote a loan document, the lender does not need to prove in court that it is genuine, and he can collect with it even from properties that were already sold.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone is bringing a proof from a known rule about loan documents. The goal is to show that the document in our case should also let the holder collect from sold properties.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a lender has to prove that a שטר is real (קיום השטר) before he can collect from buyers. If the borrower himself admits he wrote it, no proof is needed, and it collects from נכסים משועבדים. The argument is that in our case the seller also admits the document, so it should work the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Admits to a document: the signer agrees that he wrote it
To prove the document is real in court (קיום השטר)
Properties that were sold to others but are still under a lien (שעבוד) for the debt

phrases.english: One who admits about a document that he wrote it –
the holder does not need to prove it valid in court,
and he collects from liened properties that were sold.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹדֶה בִּשְׁטָר שֶׁכְּתָבוֹ אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְקַיְּימוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes an argument that began before this section.
steps.raayaObject: That the document in our case lets the holder collect from נכסים משועבדים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The accepted rule that a שטר the borrower admits writing needs no קיום and collects from משועבדים.

steps.title: רבא: a real loan document is different from a deal that should never have been written
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the comparison. A loan document records something allowed. Our document records a deal that should never have been written.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Are these the same? There, the document was allowed to be written. Here, it was not allowed to be written.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on the proof from Step 1 by showing the two cases are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting a document only helps when the document records something real and legitimate. A loan really happened, so the שטר stands. Our document records an improper deal, so it has no strength to take from buyers. The signer's admission cannot fix that.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they comparable? A phrase used to reject a comparison
Was allowed to be written; the document records a legitimate matter
There / here: used to contrast two cases

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's key idea: a document only collects from משועבדים if it was נִיתַּן לְהִכָּתֵב, meaning it records something that was properly allowed to be written.

phrases.english: Rava said to him: Are these comparable?
There, it was allowed to be written.
phrases.notes: "There" means the loan document from the step before.

phrases.english: Here, it was not allowed to be written.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא מִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between a loan document and our sale document.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The loan document records a legitimate matter. Ours records a deal that should never have been written.

steps.title: רבינא challenges with רבי יוחנן's rule on backdated documents
steps.stepSummary: מרימר taught רבא's idea. רבינא asked: if so, why did רבי יוחנן need a גזירה for a backdated document? He could simply have said it was 'not allowed to be written'.
steps.simpleTranslation: מרימר sat and taught this teaching. רבינא said to מרימר: But then take what רבי יוחנן said, that a backdated document is invalid because of a rabbinic decree, in case the lender collects from the earlier date. Let us say instead that it is invalid because it was not allowed to be written!
steps.whatsHappening: First the גמרא sets the scene: מרימר is teaching רבא's idea. Then רבינא attacks it from a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said a שטר מוקדם (a backdated loan document) is invalid only because of a גזירה, so that the lender won't take from buyers using the false early date. רבינא argues that if רבא's rule were true, רבי יוחנן would not need a גזירה at all. A backdated document is plainly 'not allowed to be written', so it should be invalid on its own merits.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to prevent a problem
The first, earlier date written on a backdated document

phrases.english: Mareimar sat and was stating this teaching.
phrases.notes: "This teaching" is רבא's line from Step 2.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Mareimar:
But that which Rabbi Yochanan said,
"a decree, lest he collect from the first date",
let us say instead: it was not allowed to be written!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְמָרִימָר אֶלָּא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's principle from Step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's principle of לא ניתן ליכתב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that principle were true, רבי יוחנן would have used it for the backdated document instead of needing a גזירה.

steps.title: A backdated document is still valid from its true date
steps.stepSummary: מרימר answers that a backdated document is wrong only about the early date. From the real date it is fine. Our document is not valid at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: How can you compare them? There, true, it was not allowed to be written from the first date, but it was allowed to be written from the second date. Here, it was not allowed to be written at all.
steps.whatsHappening: מרימר defends רבא's rule by showing that the backdated document is only partly 'not allowed to be written'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A backdated loan document records a real loan. Only the date is wrong, so it is still good from the true, later date. That is why רבי יוחנן needed a גזירה to stop people from collecting from the early date. Our document has no valid part at all, so it is completely 'לא ניתן ליכתב'.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you say that? Used to reject a comparison as not similar
The second, true date when the loan actually happened

phrases.english: He said to him: How can you compare?

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם נְהִי דְּלֹא נִיתַּן לִיכָּתֵב מִזְּמַן רִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: There, granted that it was not allowed to be written from the first date,
but it was allowed to be written from the second date.
Here, it was not allowed to be written at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge from Step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (partial vs. total invalidity).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A backdated document is just as 'not allowed to be written' as our document.
steps.terutzMaskana: A backdated document is valid from the true date, so a גזירה was needed. Our document is invalid entirely.

steps.title: Challenge from the robber who sold a stolen field
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that a buyer of a stolen field, when the field is taken away, collects his principal from the robber's sold properties. Why doesn't 'לא ניתן ליכתב' block that?
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about what was taught in a ברייתא: How does collecting for the improvement of land work? A man robbed a field from his friend, sold it to someone else, and the buyer improved it. Then the field is taken away from the buyer. When the buyer collects from the robber, he collects the principal from sold properties, and he collects the improvement only from free properties. Let us say there too: it was not allowed to be written!
steps.whatsHappening: A second challenge to רבא's rule, this time from a ברייתא. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling a stolen field is clearly a deal that should never have been written. Even so, the ברייתא lets the buyer collect the money he paid (the קרן) from the robber's נכסים משועבדים. This seems to show that 'לא ניתן ליכתב' does not block collecting from buyers, which contradicts רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: The improvement or increased value of land
Taken out of his possession (returned to the real owner)
Free properties that the seller still owns and has not sold

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא splits the payment. The קרן can be taken even from buyers (משועבדים), but the שבח only from what the robber still owns (בני חורין). The challenge is about the קרן part.

phrases.english: But that which is taught in a baraita:
Regarding enhancement of land, how does it work?
Say that one robbed a field from his fellow
and sold it to another, and that buyer enhanced it,
and it is taken out of his possession.
When he (the buyer) collects from the robber –
he collects the principal from liened properties,
and the enhancement he collects from free properties.
Let us say: it was not allowed to be written!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּתַנְיָא לְשֶׁבַח קַרְקָעוֹת כֵּיצַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רבא's principle, after the first was answered in Step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's principle that a document which was לא ניתן ליכתב cannot collect from משועבדים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Selling a stolen field is a deal that should never have been written, yet the ברייתא lets the buyer collect the קרן from נכסים משועבדים.

steps.title: The robber has reasons to make the document work, our seller does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the robber case. The robber wants to fix things with the owner so the buyer's document stands. In our case the seller wants the buyer out.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare? There, in the robber case, one view says the robber doesn't want to be called a robber. Another view says he wants to keep his name as an honest man. Either way, he will make peace with the real owner and make the buyer's document valid. Here, the seller is trying to push the buyer away. Will he make the document valid for him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 5. The robber case is different, because there the document will really end up being honored.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5 the ברייתא seemed to show that a 'bad' document still lets the buyer collect from sold properties. The גמרא says the robber case is not 'bad' in the same way. Whatever the robber's motive, he will pay off the owner and make his sale document good. In our case the seller's whole goal is to get rid of the buyer, so the document is never fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'How can you compare?' The opening of a rejection that shows two cases are different
His trustworthiness, his good name for honesty
Appeases, makes peace with (here by paying the real owner)
To chase away, to push someone out

steps.whatToRemember: A document that 'should never have been written' gives no lien on sold properties. The robber case is different because the robber himself will make his sale document good.

phrases.english: How can these be compared?
There, whether according to the one who says
phrases.notes: 'There' means the ברייתא from step 5, about buying a field from a robber.

phrases.english: he prefers that the buyer not call him a robber,
or according to the one who says
he prefers to keep his good name for honesty,
he will appease the field's owner
and make his document stand.
Here, he intends to chase the buyer away from it,
will he uphold the document for him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5 by showing the robber case is different from ours.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): the robber will make the document valid, our seller will not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The robber's sale document also records something that should not have been written, yet the buyer still collects from sold properties.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the robber case the document will in the end be made valid by the robber himself. In our case the seller wants the buyer out, so the document stays invalid.

steps.title: No fixing a price for future produce until the market price is known
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה. You may not take money now for produce you will deliver later at a set price until the market price is out. Once it is out you may, even if you don't have the produce yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One may not fix a price for produce until the market price comes out. Once the market price has come out, one may fix a price. Even if this seller doesn't have the produce, someone else does.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts a new topic. It is about paying in advance for produce at a fixed price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying now for goods that come later can look like a loan. If prices go up, the buyer gets more than he paid, which can be רבית. Once there is a known market price, the seller could go buy the produce now at that price, so it counts as a normal sale, even if he himself has none.

keyTerms.meaning: Fix a price ahead of time for goods to be delivered later
The market price has 'come out,' meaning it is set and known

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the seller must already own the produce. Once the market price is known he may fix a price even if he owns none, because others have it and he could buy it.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One may not fix a price for produce
until the market price comes out.
Once the market price has come out, one may fix a price,
even though this one does not have it,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the seller; 'that one' is someone else in the market who has the produce.

phrases.english: that one has it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין פּוֹסְקִין עַל הַפֵּירוֹת עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא הַשַּׁעַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fixing a price for future produce is allowed only once the market price is known. After that it is allowed even if the seller has no produce himself.

steps.title: A seller whose goods are almost ready may fix a price early
steps.stepSummary: If the seller harvested first, before any market price, he may still fix a price for goods that are nearly finished. Examples are a grain stack, grapes, olives, potter's clay and lime in the kiln.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was the first of the reapers, he may fix a price with the buyer for a grain stack. He may also do so for a basket of grapes, a vat of olives, a potter's clay lumps, and lime once he has sunk it in the kiln.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives an exception to the rule of step 7. A seller who already has the goods almost ready may fix a price even before the market price is out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 the problem was fixing a price before the market price exists. Here the seller himself already has the goods, close to their final form. That is enough, even with no market price yet.

keyTerms.meaning: First among the reapers, the first to harvest
A large basket (here of grapes ready for pressing)
A vat where olives are kept before pressing
A kiln, an oven for baking lime or pottery

phrases.english: If he was the first among the reapers,
he may fix a price with him for the grain stack,
and for the basket of grapes,
and for the vat of olives,
and for the clay lumps of a potter,
and for lime once he has sunk it in the kiln.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה הוּא תְּחִילָּה לַקּוֹצְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the rule in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller who has the goods almost ready may fix a price even before the market price comes out.

steps.title: Fixing a price for manure, and the disagreement of רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא says a price for manure may be fixed all year. רבי יוסי says only if the seller already has manure in his dung pile. The חכמים permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He may fix a price with him for manure all year round. רבי יוסי says: one may not fix a price for manure unless he has manure in his dung pile. The חכמים permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more case, manure. It brings a disagreement over whether the seller must already have some.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Manure is always being made, so the first opinion treats it as if it is always ready. רבי יוסי is stricter: the seller must already have a pile of manure for the sale. The חכמים disagree and allow it in any case.

keyTerms.meaning: All the days of the year, any time
A dung pile, a heap of refuse

steps.whatToRemember: The basic rule is no fixing a price before the market price is out. The exceptions are goods the seller already has nearly ready, and manure. On manure, רבי יוסי requires an existing pile and the חכמים do not.

phrases.english: And he may fix a price with him for manure
all the days of the year.
Rabbi Yosei says:
One may not fix a price for manure

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הָיְתָה לוֹ זֶבֶל בָּאַשְׁפָּה,
phrases.english: unless he has manure in the dung pile,
and the Sages permit it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפוֹסֵק עִמּוֹ עַל הַזֶּבֶל כׇּל יְמוֹת הַשָּׁנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another exception, manure, and brings a disagreement about it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A price for manure may be fixed all year. רבי יוסי requires that the seller already have manure in his pile, and the חכמים permit it in all cases.

steps.title: Locking in the lowest price, and רבי יהודה's addition
steps.stepSummary: The משנה allows the buyer to fix the most favorable price. רבי יהודה says that even without such a deal, the buyer can demand the current cheap rate or his money back.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he may fix a deal with him at the best rate. רבי יהודה says: even if he did not fix the deal at the best rate, the buyer can say, 'Give me at this rate, or give me back my money.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its rules about paying now for produce that comes later. It allows the buyer to fix the best price of the season, and רבי יהודה adds a right the buyer has even without that deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part lets the buyer agree ahead of time to get the cheapest rate that will exist. רבי יהודה says that even without this agreement, if the price drops the buyer may insist on the new cheaper rate. If the seller refuses, the buyer can cancel and take back his money, because he never formally acquired the produce.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'high rate': the rate at which the most produce is given for the money, which is the cheapest price

steps.confusionAlert: 'High rate' does not mean a high price. It means a high amount of produce per coin, which is the best deal for the buyer.

phrases.english: And he may fix a price with him at the highest rate.
phrases.notes: 'Highest rate' here means the most produce for the money, so the cheapest price of the season.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא פָּסַק עִמּוֹ
phrases.english: Even though he did not fix a price with him
at the highest rate,
he can say: Give me at this rate,
or give me back my money.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפוֹסֵק עִמּוֹ בְּשַׁעַר הַגָּבוֹהַּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה that began in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer may lock in the season's cheapest rate. According to רבי יהודה, even without that deal he can demand the cheaper current rate or cancel the sale.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: no fixing a price by the market rate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with רבי יוחנן's rule, reported by רבי אסי, that you may not fix a price based on the market rate.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: you may not fix a price according to the rate in the market.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a rule from רבי יוחנן that seems to limit when a price may be fixed. The next steps will question how far this rule goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a price may be fixed once the market rate is out. רבי יוחנן says the market rate is not always a safe basis, because market prices can change. The גמרא will now explore which markets he meant.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One may not fix a price based on the rate in the market.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה's rule that a price may be fixed once the market rate is out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A price for future delivery may not be fixed according to the market rate.

steps.title: רבי זירא asks: even a big central market?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks רבי אסי whether רבי יוחנן's rule applies even to the large central market.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said to רבי אסי: Did רבי יוחנן say this even about a big market like this one?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks how wide רבי יוחנן's rule is. Does it cover even a huge, steady central market?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A big central market has a lot of supply, so its prices are fairly steady. If the rule covers even that market, it is very strict. רבי זירא wants to know its limits.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא לְרַבִּי אַסִּי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said to Rabbi Asi:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אֲפִילּוּ כַּדּוֹרְמוּס הַזֶּה?
phrases.english: Did Rabbi Yochanan say this even about a market like this big central one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא לְרַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the scope of רבי יוחנן's rule from step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רבי יוחנן's rule include a large central market?

steps.title: Only small-town markets
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי answers that רבי יוחנן meant only the small markets of towns, whose prices are not fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: רבי יוחנן said this only about the market of small towns, because their prices are not steady.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אסי limits רבי יוחנן's rule to small-town markets.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Small markets have little supply, so their prices jump up and down. You cannot rely on such a price. A big market's price is steady enough to rely on.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule is about unsteady small-town prices, not big steady markets.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
phrases.english: He said to him: Rabbi Yochanan said this only
about the market of small towns,
since their prices are not steady.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule covers only small-town markets with unsteady prices.

steps.title: Under the first reading, when does the משנה ever apply?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if we had kept the first idea, that רבי יוחנן forbids even the big market, how could the משנה allow fixing a price once the rate is out?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to what we first thought, that רבי יוחנן said this even about the big market, then the משנה that teaches 'You may not fix a price on produce until the rate is out; once the rate is out you may fix' — when could that ever happen?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first idea for a moment. It asks how the משנה would make sense under it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה clearly allows fixing a price once the market rate is out. If רבי יוחנן banned relying on every market, even a big one, there would be no case left where the משנה's permission applies. So the first reading seems to clash with the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: What came up in our mind, what we first thought
How can you find such a case?

phrases.english: And according to what we thought at first,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אֲפִילּוּ כַּדּוֹרְמוּס הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yochanan said it even about this big market,
then the משנה that teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין פּוֹסְקִין עַל הַפֵּירוֹת עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא הַשַּׁעַר,
phrases.english: One may not fix a price on produce until the market rate is out,
once the rate is out, one may fix a price,
how can you find such a case?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דִּסְלֵיק אַדַּעְתִּין מֵעִיקָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבי זירא's first idea and tests it against the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first reading of רבי יוחנן, that he forbade relying even on a big market.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If no market rate can be relied on, the משנה's permission to fix a price once the rate is out would never apply.

steps.title: The משנה means wheat from warehouses and ships
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה could be talking about wheat sold in bulk from warehouses and ships, whose price lasts longer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is talking about wheat from warehouses and ships, whose price stays the same for longer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that even under the first reading, the משנה can still apply to one special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wheat that arrives in huge loads from storehouses and ships keeps a steady price for a long time. So even if ordinary market rates cannot be trusted, this rate can. The משנה's permission works for that kind of wheat.

phrases.english: The משנה is about wheat from warehouses and ships,
whose price lasts longer.
phrases.notes: So much of this wheat comes in at once that its price does not jump around.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִיתִין בְּחִיטֵּי דְּאַכְלַבֵּי וְאַרְבֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the משנה to a special situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the first reading, the משנה would seem to have no case where it applies.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה applies to bulk wheat from warehouses and ships, whose price is steady.

steps.title: ברייתא: the seller may fix a price even without produce
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא repeats the rule of the משנה and gives the reason: even if this seller has no produce, someone else has it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: you may not fix a price on produce until the rate is out. Once the rate is out you may fix a price, because even if this one does not have the produce, that one has it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains why a seller who has no produce may still fix a price once the rate is out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that fixing a price ahead of time looks like interest. Once the rate is out, the seller could buy the produce right now from someone else at that rate. So it is as if he already has it.

keyTerms.meaning: This one does not have it, but that one has it

steps.whyThisMatters: This reason explains the whole rule: what matters is that the produce is available in the market, not that this seller owns it.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין פּוֹסְקִין עַל הַפֵּירוֹת עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא הַשַּׁעַר,
phrases.english: One may not fix a price on produce until the market rate is out,
once the rate is out, one may fix a price,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לָזֶה יֵשׁ לָזֶה.
phrases.english: because even though this one does not have it, that one has it.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the seller and 'that one' is someone else in the market who has the produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that explains the משנה from step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the rate is out, a price may be fixed even by a seller without produce, since the produce is available from others.

steps.title: New and old grain at different prices
steps.stepSummary: If new grain sells at four and old grain at three, a price may not be fixed until a rate is out for both.
steps.simpleTranslation: If new grain was selling at four and old grain at three, you may not fix a price until the rate is out for both the new and the old.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a case where two kinds of grain have two different prices.
steps.deeperAnalysis: New grain is cheaper here: four measures for a coin, against three for old grain. By the time of delivery the new grain will no longer be new, and it may cost the same as old grain. So a price may not be fixed by the cheap new-grain rate until a rate is out for both the new and the old.

keyTerms.meaning: New grain, from this year's harvest

steps.whatToRemember: A fixed price must rest on a steady, real market rate. Unsteady small-town prices, or a gap between new and old grain, do not count.

phrases.english: If new grain was at four and old grain at three –
phrases.notes: Four סאה for a סלע for new grain, three for old. More measures per coin means a cheaper price.

phrases.english: one may not fix a price until the rate is out
for both the new and the old.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ חֲדָשׁוֹת מֵאַרְבַּע וִישָׁנוֹת מִשָּׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a further case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When new and old grain have different prices, a price may not be fixed until a rate is out for both.

steps.title: Gleaners' wheat and regular wheat need separate prices
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a case: gleaners' wheat sells at four סאה for a סלע and everyone else's at three. A price may not be fixed until a rate is out for both the gleaner and the ordinary seller.
steps.simpleTranslation: If gleaners' wheat sells at four סאה for a סלע, and everyone else's sells at three, we do not fix a price until the market rate is out for the gleaner and for the regular seller.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going with another case like the one before it (new grain and old grain). This time the two kinds of wheat are gleaners' wheat and regular wheat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Gleaners' wheat is cheaper because it is gathered from many fields and is lower quality. Since there are two separate prices, each kind of wheat needs its own known market rate before anyone may fix a price for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Gleaners: poor people who gather leftover grain from fields
Fixing a price now for produce to be delivered later

phrases.english: If the gleaners were selling at four,
phrases.notes: Four סאה of wheat for one סלע. A lower price means more wheat for the same money.

phrases.english: and for every other person at three –
we do not fix a price until the rate goes out
for the gleaner and for the regular seller.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ לָקוֹטוֹת מֵאַרְבַּע, וּלְכׇל אָדָם מִשָּׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case in the same ברייתא as step 17, using gleaners' wheat and regular wheat instead of new and old grain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When gleaners' wheat and regular wheat have different prices, a price may be fixed only after a rate is out for each.

steps.title: A gleaner may fix a price at the gleaners' rate
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that gleaners may fix a price at the gleaners' rate.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: we may fix a price for gleaners at the gleaners' rate.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains how to apply the ברייתא: once the gleaners' rate is out, a gleaner may fix his price at that rate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said both rates must be out. רב נחמן focuses on the gleaner: he only needs the gleaners' rate. He does not have to wait for the regular rate.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
We fix a price for gleaners at the gleaners' rate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: פּוֹסְקִין לַלָּקוֹטוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how step 18's rule works for the gleaner himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gleaner may fix a price at the gleaners' rate once that rate is known.

steps.title: Why can't a homeowner also use the gleaners' rate?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if a gleaner may fix a price because he can borrow from another gleaner, a בעל הבית could also borrow from a gleaner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב נחמן: How is a gleaner different? If he has no wheat, he can borrow from another gleaner. A homeowner can also borrow from a gleaner!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רב נחמן. If the gleaner may fix a price because he could borrow wheat, why not let a homeowner do the same thing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason a price may be fixed is that the seller could get the wheat right now, even by borrowing it (like step 16: someone else has it). רבא argues that a בעל הבית could also borrow gleaners' wheat, so he too should be allowed to fix a price at the gleaners' rate.

keyTerms.meaning: A homeowner: an ordinary landowner who sells his own wheat

phrases.english: Rava said to Rav Naḥman:
What is different about a gleaner,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי לֵית לֵיהּ יָזֵיף מִלָּקוֹט חַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: that if he has none, he can borrow from his fellow gleaner?
A homeowner can also borrow from a gleaner!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא לָקוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's ruling in step 19 by using its own reasoning.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's limit that only gleaners may use the gleaners' rate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason, being able to borrow the wheat, applies to a homeowner just as much as to a gleaner.

steps.title: It is beneath a homeowner to borrow from a gleaner
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that a בעל הבית feels embarrassed to borrow from a gleaner, so we cannot count on him doing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: for a homeowner, it is degrading to borrow from a gleaner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers רבא. A homeowner would not really borrow from a poor gleaner, because it is embarrassing for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the seller could really get the wheat now. A gleaner would easily borrow from another gleaner. A homeowner would not lower himself to do it, so for him it does not count as wheat he can get, and he must wait for the regular rate.

keyTerms.meaning: It is degrading for him; beneath his dignity

phrases.english: He said to him:
for a homeowner, it is a degrading thing
to borrow from a gleaner.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת זִילָא בֵּיהּ מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical distinction: a homeowner would not actually borrow
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A homeowner, like a gleaner, could borrow gleaners' wheat.
steps.terutzMaskana: A homeowner would not lower himself to borrow from a gleaner, so the gleaners' wheat is not really available to him.

steps.title: A buyer from a homeowner pays for good wheat
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: whoever pays a בעל הבית expects good-quality wheat, not the poor wheat of gleaners.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: whoever gives money to a homeowner gives it for nice produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to רבא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the homeowner would borrow, gleaners' wheat would not help him. His buyer paid for high-quality wheat, so the cheaper gleaners' wheat is a different product and its rate does not apply to him.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces a second answer

steps.whatToRemember: A gleaner may use the gleaners' rate, but a homeowner may not, either because he won't borrow from a gleaner or because his buyer wants better wheat.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
whoever gives money to a homeowner –
gives it for nice produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: מַאן דְּיָהֵיב זוּזֵי לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the challenge in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction in the quality of what was sold
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Gleaners' wheat could cover a homeowner's sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: A homeowner's buyer paid for quality wheat, so gleaners' wheat does not count.

steps.title: No borrowing based on the market rate
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת quotes רב הונא: one may not borrow produce based on the market rate.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said in the name of רב הונא: we do not borrow based on the market rate.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רב הונא, this time about borrowing produce instead of buying it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Borrowing produce now and paying it back later could be רבית if prices go up. רב הונא says it is forbidden even though the produce has a known market price.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said that Rav Huna said:
We do not borrow based on the market rate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: אֵין לֹוִין עַל שַׁעַר שֶׁבַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from fixing a price on a sale to borrowing produce.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Borrowing produce based on the market rate is forbidden.

steps.title: Did רב הונא really forbid it? The students' case
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא (or רב יוסי בר אבא) challenges this. רב הונא once allowed students to borrow in תשרי and pay back in טבת, because wheat was for sale in הִינֵי and שִׁילֵי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר חמא, or some say רב יוסי בר אבא, said to רב ששת: Did רב הונא really say this? But they asked רב הונא: these yeshiva students who borrow in תשרי and pay back in טבת, is it allowed or forbidden? He told them: there is wheat in הִינֵי and wheat in שִׁילֵי. If they want, they can buy it and pay him back.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone challenges רב ששת's report, because רב הונא himself allowed this kind of borrowing in a story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא allowed the students to borrow because wheat was for sale nearby, so they could buy it and pay back at any time. That sounds like borrowing based on the market rate is allowed, which contradicts step 23.

keyTerms.meaning: Did he really say this? A sign of a contradiction

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא לְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama said to Rav Sheshet,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב יוֹסֵי בַּר אַבָּא לְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Yosei bar Abba to Rav Sheshet:
And did Rav Huna say this?
But they asked Rav Huna:
these students of the yeshiva,
who borrow in Tishrei and pay back in Tevet,
is it permitted or forbidden?
He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: הָא חִיטֵּי בְּהִינֵי וְהָא חִיטֵּי בְּשִׁילֵי,
phrases.english: there is wheat in Hini and there is wheat in Shili,
if they want, they can buy it and pay him back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַב הוּנָא הָכִי? וְהָא בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 23 by showing רב הונא allowed it in practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's report that רב הונא forbids borrowing based on the market rate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב הונא allowed the students to borrow because wheat was for sale, so he must hold that borrowing is allowed.

steps.title: רב הונא changed his mind
steps.stepSummary: At first רב הונא forbade it, but after hearing רבי אלעזר's ruling allowing it, he also allowed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first רב הונא held that we may not borrow. Once he heard what רבי שמואל בר חייא said in the name of רבי אלעזר, that we may borrow, he too said: we may borrow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that both reports of רב הונא are true, from different times. He first forbade it and later changed his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 was רב הונא's first opinion, and the students' story came after he changed. He changed because of רבי אלעזר's ruling, so in the end borrowing based on the market rate is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא first forbade borrowing based on the market rate, but changed his mind after hearing רבי אלעזר. The final ruling is that it is allowed.

phrases.aramaic: מֵעִיקָּרָא סָבַר רַב הוּנָא אֵין לֹוִין,
phrases.english: At first Rav Huna held that we do not borrow,
once he heard this

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר חִיָּיא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: לֹוִין,
phrases.english: that Rabbi Shmuel bar Ḥiyya said that Rabbi Elazar said: we may borrow,
he too said: we may borrow.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיקָּרָא סָבַר רַב הוּנָא אֵין לֹוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Retraction: the two statements come from different times
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא holds both that borrowing is forbidden and that it is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא retracted his first view and agreed with רבי אלעזר that borrowing is allowed.

steps.title: A friend offers to buy a traveler's package at the other town's price
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא describes a man carrying goods from a cheap place to an expensive place. A friend meets him and offers to take the goods and pay him the price of the expensive place.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Someone was carrying a package of goods from one place to another. His friend met him and said: Give it to me, and I will pay you the same price they would pay you in that place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new ברייתא and lays out the case. It is setting things up: the ruling on whether this deal is allowed comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The traveler plans to sell his goods where the price is higher. The friend wants the goods now but agrees to pay that higher price. Since this sugya deals with רבית, the question will be whether this deal counts as paying extra for waiting, or as a fair sale.

keyTerms.meaning: A package or bundle of goods.
"I will pay you." Literally, "I will bring up to you."

steps.confusionAlert: This piece does not give a ruling yet. Don't decide whether the deal is allowed or forbidden until you see the next line of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who carries a package from one place to another place,
his friend met him and said to him:
Give it to me, and I will pay you
the same way they would pay you in that place.
phrases.notes: "That place" is the town he is heading to, where the price is higher.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹלִיךְ חֲבִילָה מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of borrowing produce based on the market rate (steps 23-25) to a new ברייתא about selling goods at another place's price.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line only sets up the case: a buyer offers to take goods now and pay the higher price of the destination town.
